# Dancify

> Dancify is a camera, a practice diary and a video editor for dancers, for iPhone and iPad (iOS and iPadOS 26 or later, also iPhone Duo), made by AppRise Ventures Oy in Espoo, Finland. Film a take and a frame from it lands on that day in your calendar; open any day to loop a part, slow it down, count it, edit it or set it beside your first try. The app is in English, German, Finnish, Spanish, French and Japanese. Free to download, with no account, no ads and no tracking; Dancify Premium adds progress reels, side-by-side compare and the pose guide.

## What Dancify does

Dancify is built around one loop: film a practice, see it on your calendar, then edit, loop and compare. Its promise is that every practice is kept, and progress shows up as your own footage rather than scores.

- Camera for dancers (free): a musical count-in ("5, 6, 7, 8") at a set tempo with a click and haptics so you can walk to your mark; lenses and zoom (0.5×, 1×, 2×, pinch, zoom dial), tap to focus, hold to lock focus and exposure; Follow: tap a dancer and focus and exposure stay on them as they move, with an optional Keep in frame zoom and support for DockKit motorised stands that turn to follow; HD or 4K at 30 or 60 fps, slow motion at 120 or 240 fps; mirror, torch, grid and level, auto-stop, record with the volume buttons or Camera Control
- Hands-free (free): raise a hand beside your head and hold it still; the take is kept and the next count-in starts, right from your mark
- Practise with a reference (free): play a reference video (your own take, or a video from Photos or Files) picture-in-picture or side by side while filming, starting on the count-in's downbeat; it stays out of the recording's sound unless headphones are connected
- Practice diary (free): a calendar where each day shows a frame from what you danced; log classes and rehearsals without video; notes, tags, favourites and milestones; a timeline with filters; pieces (choreographies) with every take in order; a month review
- Player (free): slow motion down to 0.25×, frame-by-frame, mirror, an A–B loop with an optional eight-count pause, a counts overlay (1–8 in time with the music, tempo and the 1 found in the take's music, or tap your own, jump by eight-counts), full screen, AirPlay and external displays
- Editor (free): frame-accurate trim and split, reorder and duplicate, speed from 0.25× to 2× (fine control to 4×) with ramps, freeze frames, crop, rotate, straighten and mirror, colour and light adjustments with looks, titles, captions, a date stamp and a count overlay, a music track from Files with fades, markers, undo and redo; exports as a new take, so the original is never changed; share or save to Photos
- Dancify Premium: progress reel export (first try to latest, with dates; sequence, side-by-side or grid layouts; 9:16 for TikTok, Reels and Shorts, or 4:5, 1:1 and 16:9; saves to Photos, copies the caption and opens the app), side-by-side compare of two takes played together and lined up to their music, and the pose guide (lines over the body for shoulders, hips and balance, drawn on the device with Apple's Vision framework). Yearly with a one-week free trial, or monthly
- Siri and Shortcuts: Record practice, Log practice, Open today, Show progress for a piece
- Private by design: no account, no ads, no analytics, no tracking. Videos and the diary stay on the device; optional iCloud sync uses the person's own private iCloud (CloudKit), videos included, which the developer can't see. App Store privacy label: Data Not Collected

Suits ballet, contemporary, jazz, hip-hop, heels, K-pop covers, salsa and bachata, ballroom, tap, Irish dance, commercial and cheer.

# How to film yourself dancing: angles, light and setup

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/
Published: 2026-11-03 · Updated: 2026-11-03 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> The run felt clean, then the video showed bent knees and cropped feet. Here's how to set up a phone so it shows what matters: height and distance for each style, light, sound, stands and what to film.

Every dancer knows the moment: the run felt clean, then the video shows a bent supporting knee, a late arm and feet that never quite pointed. Filming yourself is the most honest teacher you'll ever have, as long as the camera is set up to show what matters. Here's how to do it well with nothing more than a phone.

 The short answer

To film yourself dancing, put your phone on a stand at about hip to chest height, 3 to 5 metres away, in landscape, so your whole body fits with space above your head and below your feet. Face a window or lamp rather than standing in front of it, lock focus and exposure on yourself, play the music out loud so the timing is in the take, and film from the same spot every time.

- Height: hip height for ballet and heels, chest height for hip-hop and K-pop, knee height for tap, Irish and floor work.
- Framing: head to toe plus the space you travel in. Cropped feet hide half of what you came to check.
- Light: in front of you or to the side, never behind. Backlight turns you into a silhouette.

## Why film your practice at all?

The mirror shows you one angle, live, while you're busy dancing. Video shows you every angle you choose, afterwards, when you can actually look. You can slow it down, watch the feet only, then watch the arms only, and see the same eight-count ten times without getting tired.

It works, too. In a small study with three competitive dancers, watching and scoring their own videos against a checklist improved every move the researchers tracked, and the dancers found the method easy to keep up.[1] Three dancers isn't a big sample, but anyone who has taught with a camera in the room will recognise the result: people correct what they can see.

## Set up in five minutes: step by step

-

Clear and mark your space. Decide where "front" is and put a small piece of tape on the floor where you start. Every take from the same mark makes takes comparable weeks later.

-

Choose the orientation. Landscape for practice: it gives you room to travel sideways and keeps your feet in frame on a jump. Portrait only when you're making a vertical video for social media, or for a K-pop cover filmed like a fancam.

-

Set the height. Roughly the middle of your body. Too high (a phone on a shelf looking down) shortens your legs and hides your lines; too low exaggerates jumps but distorts your head. See the table below for each style.

-

Step back to frame head to toe. Stand on your mark, raise your arms, then do your biggest travelling step. You should stay in frame with a little space above your fingertips and below your feet. In most living rooms that means 3 to 5 metres, or the 0.5× wide lens if you can't go back further.

-

Fix the light. Face the window or put a lamp behind the camera. Turn off any light that shines straight into the lens.

-

Lock focus and exposure on you. On an iPhone, press and hold on yourself in the preview. Otherwise the camera keeps refocusing on the sofa every time you turn.

-

Play the music out loud. Put the speaker near the phone so the recording carries the beat. Without music in the take, you can't check your timing later.

-

Record a ten-second test. Watch it back once before the real take. It's the cheapest fix there is.

## Camera height and distance by dance style

Every style has something it needs to see. Start here, then adjust for your room.

| Style | Camera height | Framing | What to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ballet | Hip height | Full body, feet clearly on the floor; a second take from the side for arabesques | Turnout, pointed feet, supporting knee, hips square |
| Contemporary and floor work | Knee to hip height | Wide (0.5×), extra floor in front of you | Transitions to and from the floor, use of weight |
| Hip-hop and commercial | Chest height | Full body with room to travel; landscape | Grooves on the beat, hits, levels, clean stops |
| K-pop covers | Chest height | Centred, front-on like a stage camera; portrait is fine | Formation spot, angles of arms, facial expression |
| Heels | Hip height, slightly low | Full body including shoes | Ankle stability, lines, walks |
| Salsa, bachata, ballroom | Chest height | Both partners head to toe, 4 to 6 metres back | Frame, footwork timing, connection |
| Tap and Irish | Knee height | Full body, but the feet are the priority; mic near the floor | Clarity of sounds, ankle work, timing |

Heights are starting points. Whatever you choose, write it down and reuse it, so every take is filmed the same way.

## Which angle: front, side or behind?

Front is the default because it's how an audience sees you. But it hides depth: an arabesque that looks high from the front can be dropping at the hip, and a lunge can be hanging over the knee. Use a few angles on purpose:

- Front: formations, facings, arms, expression. Your main take.
- Side (90°): posture, alignment, how high a leg really is, how deep a plié really goes.
- Front corner (45°): the most flattering and most honest at once, great for showcase runs.
- From behind: when you're learning from a video, filming from behind means you and the teacher face the same way, so left is left.

If you want to compare your progress later, pick one angle as your "record" angle and never change it. Same spot, same height, same lens. Our guide to [making a dance progress video](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-progress-video/) explains why that consistency matters more than anything else.

## Light, frame rate and sound

Light. Daylight from a window in front of you or at 45° is the best free light you have. Overhead lights alone put shadows in your eyes; one lamp behind the camera fixes most of that. If you film at night, switch on every light in the room, because a dim room means a grainy, blurry video.

Frame rate. 30 fps is fine for most practice. Film at 60 fps for turns, jumps and fast footwork, so a slowed-down replay stays smooth. True slow motion (120 or 240 fps) needs a lot of light and isn't worth it for a full run; save it for checking one jump or one turn.

Sound. Play the music from a speaker next to the phone, not from earbuds. For tap and Irish, the sound is the dance: keep the phone closer and lower, and the music a little quieter, so the taps cut through.

## Phone stands that actually work

### A simple tripod

Great forRepeatable height. Look for one that reaches at least 1.5 metres, with a phone clamp that holds landscape firmly.

Watch outLightweight legs wobble on sprung floors when you jump. Spread the legs wide.

### A motorised stand

Great forTravelling choreography. Stands that work with Apple's DockKit turn to keep a person in frame.[2]

Watch outIt follows one person. In a duet or a group, frame wide and keep it still.

No stand at all? A bookshelf with the phone propped against a stack of books works, as does a chair on a table. Just check the height again, and tape the spot so you can find it next time.

## What to film in each practice

Filming everything means watching nothing. A simple rhythm that works for most dancers:

- One full runFrom the top, with music, at performance energy. This is your record of the day.
- One problem sectionThe eight-counts that keep going wrong, filmed two or three times, so you can see if the fix is working.
- One noteA sentence about what you noticed. It's the start of a [dance practice journal](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/), and it's what makes a pile of videos useful.

If you're still learning the piece, filming the section you just learned is the fastest way to find out what you actually remember. More on that in [how to learn choreography faster](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-learn-choreography-faster/).

## Six mistakes that ruin dance videos

- Cutting off the feetThe most common one. Step back or switch to the wide lens until there's floor below your toes.
- Standing in front of a windowThe camera exposes for the bright window and you go dark. Turn around so the window lights you.
- Zooming in digitallyPinching past the lens you're on makes the picture soft. Move the phone closer instead.
- Filming without musicWithout the beat in the take, you can't check timing, which is half of what you need to see.
- Rushing to your markHitting record and sprinting back gives you a messy first eight. Use a count-in or a timer.
- Changing the setup every timeNew angle, new height, new room: you can't compare the takes. Keep one setup as your record.

## How Dancify helps

We built Dancify's camera for exactly this, because the standard camera app wasn't made for someone who has to run to a mark across the room.

 Free in Dancify A camera that waits for the count Hit record and a musical count-in ("5, 6, 7, 8") at your tempo gives you time to walk to your mark. Tap yourself to Follow: focus and exposure stay on you as you move, and Keep in frame can zoom gently to hold you. With a DockKit stand, the stand turns with you.

- HD or 4K, 30 or 60 fps, slow motion at 120 or 240 fps
- Mirror, grid and level, auto-stop, record with the volume buttons

You can also play a reference video, your teacher's or your own earlier take, picture-in-picture or side by side while you film, starting on the count-in's downbeat. Every take lands on that day in your calendar, so the videos become a diary instead of a camera roll. Recording, the calendar and the editor are free; videos stay on your device, or in your own iCloud if you switch sync on.

 Film your next practice

## Questions, answered

### What is the best angle to film yourself dancing?

Straight on from the front, with the phone at about hip to chest height, is the best main angle because it's how an audience sees you. Add a side angle now and then to check posture and the real height of your legs, and film from behind when you're learning from a video so left and right match.

### How far away should the camera be when filming dance?

Usually 3 to 5 metres for one dancer, and 4 to 6 metres for a couple. The test is simple: on your mark, with your arms up and on your biggest travelling step, you should stay in frame with space above your hands and below your feet. If the room is too small, use the 0.5× wide lens and stay near the centre of the frame.

### Should I film dance videos in portrait or landscape?

Landscape for practice, because it leaves room to travel and keeps your feet in frame. Portrait is fine for videos made for social media, or K-pop covers filmed front-on like a fancam, as long as your whole body fits.

### How do I film myself dancing without a tripod?

Prop the phone on a bookshelf against a stack of books, or on a chair placed on a table, so it sits at about hip to chest height. Lean it back slightly, check the framing with a short test, and mark the spot with tape so you can set up the same way next time.

### What frame rate should I use to record dance practice?

30 fps is fine for most practice. Use 60 fps for turns, jumps and fast footwork so slowed-down replays stay smooth. Save 120 or 240 fps slow motion for checking a single jump or turn, in good light.

### Does watching videos of yourself really improve your dancing?

It helps you see what you can't feel. In a small study of three competitive dancers, scoring their own videos against a checklist improved every move that was tracked. Video works best alongside a teacher's feedback, not instead of it.

## Sources

- Giambrone J, Miltenberger RG (2020). Using video self-evaluation to enhance performance in competitive dancers. Behavior Analysis in Practice 13(2), 445–453. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7314870/
- Apple Developer Documentation: DockKit, interacting with motorised stands that track subjects on camera. Apple. Checked 2026-11-04. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/dockkit

# How to learn choreography faster (and actually remember it)

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-learn-choreography-faster/
Published: 2026-11-01 · Updated: 2026-11-01 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Quick learners aren't magic. They map the piece, learn it in eight-counts, mark before they dance full out and check themselves on video. The method, step by step, with a 45-minute session plan.

Some dancers seem to pick up a combination after two run-throughs. It isn't magic and it usually isn't talent. They watch in a particular way, break the piece into pieces, mark before they dance it full out, and check themselves on video. All of that can be learned. Here's the method, from the first viewing to the night before the show.

 The short answer

To learn choreography faster, watch the whole piece once, then learn it in chunks of one or two eight-counts: feet first, then arms, then details. Mark each chunk small before dancing it full out, say the counts out loud, chain each new chunk onto the ones before, and film yourself to check against the reference. Slow the video down for the hard parts, and review the next day.

- Chunk: one or two eight-counts at a time, added on to what you already know.
- Mark: walking it through small isn't lazy. In one study, marked practice led to better performance.[1]
- Check: film each chunk; your memory of a move and the move itself are often different.

## Watch the whole piece first

Before you learn a single step, watch the full routine, or as much as you've been given, two or three times without moving. You're making a map:

- Sections: intro, verse, chorus, bridge, ending. Give each one a name you'll remember ("the floor bit", "the canon").
- Repeats: a chorus that comes back three times is one thing to learn, not three. Choreographers repeat more than it seems.
- Count it: how many eight-counts per section? Knowing "the verse is four eights" tells you when you're lost.
- Travel and facings: where on the floor does each section happen, and which way are you facing?

Experienced dancers lean on structure without thinking about it. In a classic study, young expert ballet dancers recalled choreographed sequences much better than random ones, and music at recall helped them hold on to the end of the sequence.[2] The map gives your memory something to hang on to.

## Learn in chunks of eight

-

Pick one or two eight-counts. Never more. If a single eight is dense, take it four counts at a time.

-

Feet first. Weight changes, direction and timing. Get the floor pattern right before anything else.

-

Then arms. Add the upper body once the feet are automatic. Trying both at once is where most combinations fall apart.

-

Then the details. Head, focus, hands, dynamics, the face. This is what makes it the choreography and not just the steps.

-

Say the counts. Out loud, with the accents: "five, six, seven-and-eight". Or the sound words your teacher uses ("boom, ta, pssh"). Speaking it builds a second memory alongside the body.

-

Chain it on. Learn chunk two, then dance one into two. Learn three, then one into two into three. The joins are where people forget, so practise the joins.

Start somewhere other than the top. If you always run from the beginning, the first eight gets twenty repetitions and the last one gets two. Start some runs from the middle or the last section, so the ending is as solid as the opening.

## Mark it before you dance it

Marking means walking through the choreography with reduced movement: hands sketching the arms, small steps for jumps, the head showing the turns. Dancers have always done it to save energy, but it seems to help the memory too. When dance students practised one routine full out and another by marking, they performed the marked routine better.[1] The researchers' explanation: with less physical effort to manage, there's more attention left for the order, the timing and the shapes.

A good pattern: mark a new chunk two or three times, dance it full out once, mark it again while you fix what went wrong, then dance it full out with the music.

## Counts or music?

Both, in that order. Counts give you structure: you know exactly where each move lands. Music gives you the feel: the accents, the breaths, the lyrics that cue a move. Learn a chunk on counts, then dance it to the track at once, so the counts get attached to the sound. If counting itself is the hard part, our guide to [counting music in dance](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-count-music-in-dance/) explains eight-counts, "and" counts and finding the one.

One trick from teachers: pick out landmarks in the music. "The arm goes up on the word 'fire'" sticks better than "on 6 of the third eight".

## Mirror or no mirror?

The mirror is a wonderful tool for learning shapes. It can also become a crutch. A 2024 study of ballet dancers summarises earlier work by Radell and colleagues suggesting that performance and skill learning may suffer when the mirror is the main source of feedback, and the authors recommend training both with and without it.[3]

- Learning from a video: if the teacher faces you, mirror the video so their right is your right. If they face away, you can follow directly.
- Once you know a chunk: turn away from the mirror, or face a wall, and dance it from memory. That's what the stage will feel like.
- Then film it: the camera is a mirror you can look at after you've finished dancing.

## Slow it down, loop it, film it

Speed is the last thing to add. Most fast choreography is unlearnable at tempo and easy at half speed.

| Stage | Video speed | What you're doing |
|---|---|---|
| Decode | 0.25× to 0.5× | Working out what the feet and arms actually do, frame by frame if needed |
| Learn | 0.5× to 0.75× | Dancing along, marking, saying the counts |
| Clean | 0.75× to 1× | Full out, fixing details, adding dynamics |
| Perform | 1× | From the top, with the music, no stopping |

Loop the one eight-count that keeps going wrong instead of running the whole piece again. Ten loops of the hard part beat three full runs.

Then film each chunk as soon as you think you have it. The video answers questions memory can't: is the arm really at shoulder height? Is the turn on 7 or on 7-and? Put your take next to the reference and look for one difference at a time. Our guide to [filming yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/) covers the camera setup.

## Between practices: listen, visualise, sleep

Listen to the track on repeat. On the bus, washing up, anywhere. You want to know what comes next in the music before your body has to.

Run it in your head. Mental practice has a measurable, positive effect on performance in a large meta-analysis, though how much depends on the task.[4] Imagine dancing it at full speed from your own eyes, counts and all. It doesn't replace dancing, but it's practice you can do anywhere.

Sleep on it, then review. Motor learning keeps settling overnight; in one study, a practised movement sequence was about 20% faster after sleep.[5] Start the next practice by dancing yesterday's chunks before learning new ones.

## A 45-minute learning session

- 5 min: reviewMark and then dance everything you learned last time, with the music.
- 25 min: new chunksTwo to four new eight-counts: decode slowly, mark, count, dance, chain.
- 10 min: film and checkOne take of everything so far. Watch it once, note one fix.
- 5 min: write it downWhere you stopped, what's shaky, tomorrow's first task. That's your [practice journal](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/).

## How Dancify helps you learn a piece

We designed Dancify's practice tools around this exact routine, and they're free.

 Free in Dancify Loop the hard eight Slow any take down to 0.25×, step frame by frame, and mirror it. Set an A–B loop on the eight-count that keeps going wrong, with an optional eight-count pause before it repeats, so you can get back to your spot. The counts overlay shows 1 to 8 in time with the music.

 Free in Dancify Dance with the reference Play the class video or your own earlier take picture-in-picture or side by side while you film, starting on the count-in's downbeat. Every take goes into the piece, in order, so you can see how it came together.

 Learn your next piece

Dancify keeps the reference, the loop and every take of a piece in one place, on iPhone and iPad.

- A–B loop and counts overlay
- Reference video while you film

## Questions, answered

### How can I learn choreography faster?

Watch the whole piece first to map its sections and repeats, then learn it one or two eight-counts at a time: feet first, then arms, then details. Mark each chunk before dancing it full out, say the counts aloud, chain new chunks onto old ones, slow the video down for hard parts and film yourself to check.

### How do dancers remember long routines?

They lean on structure: named sections, repeated choruses, counts and musical landmarks such as a lyric that cues a move. Research on young ballet dancers found choreographed sequences are remembered far better than random ones, and that music helps recall. Regular review, a good night's sleep and starting runs from different sections all help too.

### Is marking choreography a good way to practise?

Yes. Marking, dancing the choreography small with reduced movement, saves energy and seems to free attention for the order, timing and shapes. In a study of dance students, the routine practised by marking was performed better than the one practised full out. Mix marking with full-out runs.

### Should I mirror a dance video when learning it?

Mirror it when the teacher in the video faces you, so their right is your right. If they face away from the camera, follow it as it is. Once you know a section, dance it facing away from any mirror and film it to check.

### What speed should I practise choreography at?

Decode new moves at 0.25× to 0.5×, learn them at 0.5× to 0.75×, clean them at 0.75× to full speed, then perform from the top at 1×. Loop the one eight-count that keeps going wrong rather than running the whole piece again.

## Sources

- Warburton EC, Wilson M, Lynch M, Cuykendall S (2013). The cognitive benefits of movement reduction: evidence from dance marking. Psychological Science 24(9), 1732–1739. Checked 2026-11-04. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613478824
- Starkes JL, Deakin JM, Lindley S, Crisp F (1987). Motor versus verbal recall of ballet sequences by young expert dancers. Journal of Sport Psychology 9(3), 222–230. Checked 2026-11-04. https://doi.org/10.1123/jsp.9.3.222
- Duboff LA, DiPasquale S, Ives SJ (2024). Investigating the effects of visual feedback on muscle activity, heart rate, RPE, and perceptions of performance in ballet dancers. International Journal of Exercise Science 17(1), 1056–1067. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11385289/
- Driskell JE, Copper C, Moran A (1994). Does mental practice enhance performance? Journal of Applied Psychology 79(4), 481–492. Checked 2026-11-04. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.79.4.481
- Walker MP, Brakefield T, Morgan A, Hobson JA, Stickgold R (2002). Practice with sleep makes perfect: sleep-dependent motor skill learning. Neuron 35(1), 205–211. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12123620/

# How to make a dance progress video that's honest and motivating

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-progress-video/
Published: 2026-10-29 · Updated: 2026-10-29 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> A before-and-after only means something if both takes were filmed the same way. How to set up, how often to film, what to compare, which layout to use and how to put it together with any editor.

Most dancers only notice their progress by accident: an old clip turns up in the camera roll and suddenly the difference is obvious. A progress video does that on purpose. It puts your first attempt and your latest one in front of you, honestly, so you can see what changed and what still needs work.

 The short answer

To make a dance progress video, film the same combination the same way at regular intervals (same spot, same camera height and distance, same music and tempo, similar clothes and light), date every take, then put the first and the latest next to each other or one after the other. The consistency is what makes the comparison honest.

- Cadence: weekly while you learn a piece, monthly for technique and flexibility.
- Compare: lines, timing, musicality and stamina, one at a time.
- Layout: side by side for detail, a sequence for the story, a grid for many dates at once.

## Why a progress video works, and when it lies

Progress in dance is slow and quiet. You don't feel the extra centimetre in your développé or the half count you stopped rushing, because you live with your body every day. Video doesn't have that problem. It remembers exactly how you looked in August, and it shows it to you without kindness or cruelty.

Watching yourself with a clear question in mind is also a proven way to improve. In a small study with three young competitive dancers, scoring their own videos step by step improved all three movements the researchers tracked, for every dancer.[1] A progress video is the long version of the same habit.

But a progress video can lie, too. A wide lens in the first clip and a closer one in the last makes your legs look longer. A dark room then a sunny one changes how clean your lines look. A different song changes your energy. If the setup changes, you're comparing setups, not dancing. That's why the rest of this guide is mostly about doing the same thing every time.

## Film it the same way every time

Pick one short combination, 16 to 32 counts, that shows what you're working on. Then fix everything around it. Write the setup down once, in your notes or a [practice journal](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/), so future you can repeat it.

- Same spot, height and lensTape a mark on the floor for you and one for the stand. Keep the phone at the same height (hip to chest for most styles) and on the same lens. Never mix 0.5× and 1×.
- Same music, same tempoUse the same track at the same speed. If you slowed it down to learn, film the progress take at the final tempo, or always at the same slower one.
- Similar clothes and lightFitted clothes in a colour that stands out from the wall, and the same light source. Face the window rather than standing in front of it.
- Same point in the sessionAfter a full warm-up, before you're tired. A take at minute 10 and one at minute 80 show two different dancers.
- The first honest takeDon't wait until you're "ready" for the first clip. The whole point is that it isn't good yet.

If you need help with the setup itself, our guide to [filming yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/) covers height, distance and light for each style.

## How often to film

Film too often and the clips all look the same. Film too rarely and you lose the thread. These intervals work for most dancers:

| What you're working on | Film a progress take | A good comparison span |
|---|---|---|
| Learning a new piece | Once a week, same section | First full run vs show week |
| Technique (turns, jumps, footwork) | Every two to four weeks | Three months |
| Flexibility (splits, extensions) | Once a month | Three to six months |
| Freestyle and musicality | Every two weeks, same song | A season |
| Coming back after a break or injury | Every week or two | Your first session back vs now |

Put the dates in your calendar like a class. Progress takes that depend on remembering are the first thing to slip.

## What to compare between takes

"Better" is too vague to see. Watch the two clips several times, one question per viewing. Slow motion and frame-by-frame help with the first two.

| Look at | What to watch | How to check it |
|---|---|---|
| Lines and placement | Knees, feet, hips square, shoulders down, arm shapes | Pause on the same pose in both takes |
| Timing | Do you land on the count, or just after it? | Watch with the sound on, step frame by frame on the accents |
| Musicality | Dynamics, holds, texture, using the whole phrase | Watch once with your eyes closed for the music, then once without sound |
| Stamina | Is the last eight as sharp as the first? | Compare the end of both takes, not the start |
| Space and travel | How far you travel, direction changes, spacing | Use your floor marks as a reference |
| Confidence | Face, focus, breath, the moments you used to hesitate | Watch at normal speed, as an audience would |

If timing is the thing you're chasing, it helps to know exactly where the counts fall. Our guide to [counting music in dance](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-count-music-in-dance/) explains eight-counts and tempo.

## Choose a layout: sequence, side by side or grid

 Best for the story

### Sequence

One take after another, full frame, each with its date. It reads like a short film of your progress, and it works well for sharing because every clip gets the whole screen.

Keep in mind: small details are hard to compare when the clips don't play at the same time.

 Best for detail

### Side by side

Then and now playing together. Start both on the same count and differences in timing and lines jump out. This is the one to watch with your teacher.

Keep in mind: each clip gets half the screen, so film in a way that keeps you large in frame.

 Best for many dates

### Grid

Four takes at once, for example months one to four. It shows a trend rather than a before and after.

Keep in mind: it only works if every take was filmed the same way.

## How to make one with any video editor

You don't need special software. A free editor that can split the screen and add text is enough. On iPhone, Apple's iMovie can place a second clip beside the first with its Split Screen overlay, or in a corner as picture in picture.[2]

-

Collect your takes. Find the first and the latest progress take, plus any in between for a grid. Note each one's date.

-

Trim to the same section. Cut each clip so it starts on the same count. Start one count early so the first movement isn't clipped.

-

Line them up. For side by side, put the older take on the left (people read left to right), add the newer one as a split-screen overlay, and nudge it until both land the first accent together.

-

Keep one soundtrack. Mute one clip so the music doesn't echo. If the takes were at the same tempo, they stay in time.

-

Add dates. A small caption in a corner, like "12 Aug" and "26 Oct", is enough. Labels like "Then" and "Now" help people who watch without sound.

-

Export and keep the originals. Save the progress video as a new file and leave the original takes untouched, so you can make another one in three months.

## Sharing it, kindly

- Share with your teacher first. A side-by-side clip and one question ("is my supporting knee better?") gets better feedback than a highlight reel.
- Ask anyone else in frame. Classmates in the background didn't agree to be in your post.
- Mind the music. Commercial tracks can be muted or blocked on some platforms. For private sharing it rarely matters.
- Keep it honest. Same setup, real dates, no speed tricks. A progress video only motivates if you believe it.

Progress is easy to miss from the inside. Two dated clips side by side make it impossible to miss.

## How Dancify does it

We built Dancify so that progress videos stop being a weekend project. Every take you film lands on its day in the calendar, and every take of a piece sits in order on that piece's page, so the first and the latest are always two taps apart.

Dates go on each clip if you want them, and you set how many seconds each take plays. The reel exports as a new video you can share. Your original recordings stay as they are.

## Questions, answered

### How do I make a dance progress video?

Choose a short combination and film it the same way at regular intervals: the same spot, camera height, distance and lens, the same music and tempo, similar clothes and light. Date every take. Then put the first and the latest take side by side or one after the other in a video editor, add the dates and export it as a new video.

### How often should I film my dance progress?

Weekly while you're learning a specific piece, every two to four weeks for technique such as turns and jumps, and monthly for flexibility. Three months is usually long enough for a technique comparison to show a clear difference.

### Is side by side or before-and-after better for comparing dance videos?

Side by side is better for detail, because both takes play at the same time and differences in timing and lines are easy to see. A sequence, one take after the other, tells the story better and suits sharing. A grid works when you want to show four or more dates at once.

### What should I look for when comparing two dance videos?

Look at one thing per viewing: lines and placement, timing against the counts, musicality and dynamics, stamina at the end of the combination, how you use space, and confidence. Pause on the same pose in both takes and step frame by frame through the accents.

### Can I make a dance progress video for free?

Yes. Any editor that can split the screen and add text works, for example iMovie on iPhone with its Split Screen overlay. In Dancify, filming, the calendar and the editor are free; progress reel export and side-by-side compare are part of Dancify Premium.

### Why does my progress video not look like progress?

Usually because something in the setup changed: a different lens or distance, different light, a different song or tempo, or a take filmed at the end of a tiring session. Fix the setup and film again; and remember that consistency, timing and confidence are progress too, even when the shapes look similar.

## Sources

- Giambrone J, Miltenberger RG (2020). Using video self-evaluation to enhance performance in competitive dancers. Behavior Analysis in Practice 13(2), 445–453. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7314870/
- Apple Support: Add video overlay effects (split screen, picture in picture) in iMovie on iPhone. Apple. Checked 2026-11-04. https://support.apple.com/guide/imovie-iphone/add-video-overlay-effects-kna831efee4d/ios

# How to count music in dance: eight-counts, "5, 6, 7, 8" and finding the one

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-count-music-in-dance/
Published: 2026-10-28 · Updated: 2026-10-28 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Why do teachers start at five? Where is one? What's an "and"? Beats, bars, eight-counts and phrases explained, plus waltz, salsa and swing counts, tempo by style and five drills.

"Five, six, seven, eight!" is the first thing most of us hear in a dance class, and for a lot of beginners it's also the most confusing. Why start at five? Where is "one"? And what is an "and"? Counting music is a skill like a pirouette: a few rules, then lots of practice. Here are the rules.

 The short answer

Most dance music is in 4/4 time: four beats to a bar. Dancers count two bars together as one eight-count, 1 to 8, and four eight-counts usually make a musical phrase. "5, 6, 7, 8" is the lead-in: the last four counts before the dance starts on the next 1. An "and" is the half-beat between two counts, and waltzes are in 3/4, counted 1-2-3.

- Beat: the steady pulse you tap your foot to. Each beat is one count.
- Eight-count: eight beats, two bars of 4/4. The unit choreography is built in.
- Phrase: usually four eight-counts (32 beats). New sections of a song tend to start at the top of a phrase.

## Beats, bars and eight-counts

Musicians organise music into bars (measures). The time signature says how many beats are in each bar: 4/4 means four beats per bar, 3/4 means three.[1] Almost all pop, hip-hop, jazz, K-pop, house and Latin music is in 4/4.

Musicians count each bar "1, 2, 3, 4". Dancers count two bars together, "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8", because most dance steps and combinations take longer than one bar to finish. One eight-count is one sentence of movement; four of them make a paragraph, the phrase.

| Term | In 4/4 music | How dancers say it |
|---|---|---|
| Beat | One pulse | One count: "1" |
| Half-beat | Between two beats | "and": "1 and 2 and" |
| Bar | 4 beats | Half an eight-count |
| Eight-count | 2 bars, 8 beats | "1 to 8", "one eight" |
| Phrase | Usually 8 bars, 32 beats | "Four eights" |

## What "5, 6, 7, 8" means

When a teacher calls "5, 6, 7, 8", they're counting the second half of an eight-count out loud, in the tempo of the music, so everyone starts together on the next 1. It does three jobs at once: it tells you the tempo, it tells you exactly when "1" will land, and it gives you four counts to get ready. Teachers count only the last four because counting all eight would waste time; the first four are usually silent or just "and".

The first step of the choreography falls on 1, not on 8. Unless the teacher says "and" before 1, which means the movement starts on the half-beat before: a pick-up.

## How to find the beat and the one

-

Find the pulse. Listen for the kick drum or the bass. Tap your foot or nod your head along. Don't count yet.

-

Find the backbeat. In most pop and hip-hop, the snare or clap hits on 2 and 4. The beats between, where the kick usually sits, are 1 and 3.

-

Count to four. Say "1, 2, 3, 4" with the beats, with the snare on 2 and 4. When it feels right, it will feel like the music is leaning on your "1".

-

Join two bars into eight. Keep going "5, 6, 7, 8". If 1 doesn't feel like a fresh start, shift by four counts.

-

Find the big one. Listen for where something changes: the vocals come in, a cymbal crash, the chorus starts, a drum fill ends. That moment is almost always 1 of a phrase. Count four eights from there and you'll usually land on the next change.

Watch out for half phrases. Songs don't always keep neat 32-count phrases. A bridge might add an extra four counts, or an intro might be one bar short. If your counting drifts out of line with the music, start again from the next obvious change. Choreographers count these places specially, so ask.

## "And" counts and syncopation

Between every two counts there's an "and": "1 and 2 and 3 and". Fast footwork splits it further: "1 e and a", four sounds per beat. Any move that lands on an "and" instead of a number is off the beat, or syncopated.

- Ball change on "and-1": the quick weight change before a step.
- "Hit on the and of 4": a sharp accent just before the next bar, very common in hip-hop and commercial choreography.
- Holds: syncopation also means not moving on a count you'd expect, then catching up. "Hold 5, 6, hit 6-and" is all about the silence.

When an eight-count feels slippery, slow the music down and say every "and" out loud. Once the timing is in your mouth, it gets into your feet.

## Waltz, salsa, swing: when it's not just 1 to 8

- Waltz and 3/4Three beats per bar: "1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3". The 1 is strong, so it carries the step down. Ballet teachers often count waltzes in sixes, two bars at a time, or "and-a-1" for the pick-up.
- SalsaCounted in eights but stepped on six: "1, 2, 3, (4), 5, 6, 7, (8)". Dancing "on1" breaks forward on 1; "on2" breaks on 2.
- Bachata"1, 2, 3, tap, 5, 6, 7, tap". The tap or hip accent on 4 and 8 marks the bar.
- Cha-cha"2, 3, 4-and-1": the chassé lives on 4-and-1, which is why the dance feels like it starts on two.
- Swing and jiveMany basics are six counts long over 4/4 music, so the pattern drifts across the eight-count. Count the pattern and the music separately until it clicks.

## Tempo and BPM by dance style

Tempo is measured in beats per minute (BPM). Ballroom competitions fix tempo ranges in bars per minute, so they convert neatly; most other styles vary from song to song, so treat those numbers as a guide.

| Style | Time | Typical tempo | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Waltz | 3/4 | 84–90 BPM (28–30 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Viennese waltz | 3/4 | 174–180 BPM (58–60 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Tango | 4/4 | 124–132 BPM (31–33 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Quickstep | 4/4 | 200–208 BPM (50–52 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Rumba | 4/4 | 100–108 BPM (25–27 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Cha-cha | 4/4 | 120–128 BPM (30–32 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Jive | 4/4 | 168–176 BPM (42–44 bars/min) | WDSF[2] |
| Salsa | 4/4 | About 160–220 BPM | SalsaVida[3] |
| Bachata | 4/4 | About 108–152 BPM | SalsaVida[3] |
| Hip-hop | 4/4 | About 60–100 BPM | Ableton[4] |

Ballet class music, contemporary, jazz and K-pop vary too widely for one range. Tap along to find the tempo of the actual track.

Why it matters for practice: learning a combination at 80% of the real tempo is one of the easiest ways to get clean, and knowing the target BPM tells you how far you have to go.

## Five drills to get better at counting

-

Count the radio. Any song, anywhere: find the 1, count eights out loud through a verse and chorus. Check that the chorus lands on a 1.

-

Clap only the 1. Count silently and clap on every 1. Then only on 1 of each phrase. It trains your sense of the big structure.

-

Say the "ands". Speak a combination's counts with every "and" while you mark it.

-

Slow and build. Practise a hard eight at a slower tempo, then raise it a few BPM at a time.

-

Film and check. Record a run with the music audible and watch whether your accents land on the counts. More in [how to film yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/).

Counting is also the backbone of learning choreography: once you can hear the eights, breaking a piece into chunks becomes natural. See [how to learn choreography faster](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-learn-choreography-faster/).

## Questions, answered

### What does "5, 6, 7, 8" mean in dance?

It's a count-in. The teacher counts the last four beats of an eight-count out loud, in the tempo of the music, so everyone starts together on the next 1. It tells you the tempo, when 1 will land, and gives you four counts to get ready.

### What is an eight-count in dance?

Eight beats of music counted 1 to 8, which is two bars of 4/4 time. Choreography is usually built and taught in eight-counts, and four eight-counts usually make one musical phrase of 32 beats.

### How do I find the one in a song?

Find the steady pulse, then the backbeat: in most pop and hip-hop the snare or clap is on 2 and 4, so 1 is the beat before the first snare. Then listen for where something changes, such as the vocals coming in or the chorus starting. That's usually 1 of a phrase.

### What does "and" mean in dance counts?

The "and" is the half-beat between two counts: "1 and 2 and". A move counted "and-1" starts just before the beat. Steps that land on an "and" instead of a number are syncopated.

### How do you count a waltz?

A waltz is in 3/4, three beats per bar, counted "1, 2, 3" with the 1 strongest. Teachers often count two bars as six, or use "and-a-1" for a pick-up into the bar. Competition waltz is played at 28 to 30 bars per minute, about 84 to 90 beats per minute.

### What BPM is good for dance practice?

It depends on the style: about 84 to 90 BPM for a slow waltz, 120 to 128 for cha-cha, roughly 160 to 220 for salsa. When learning, practise a combination a little slower than the real tempo, then raise it step by step until you can dance it at the track's speed.

## Sources

- Measures and time signatures. Music Appreciation 1, Lumen Learning. Checked 2026-11-04. https://courses.lumenlearning.com/music-app-rford/chapter/measures-and-time-signatures/
- WDSF Professional Division Competition Rules, rule 9: Maximum duration of dances; tempi. World DanceSport Federation. Checked 2026-11-04. https://cdnb.worlddancesport.org/legacy-docs/wdsf/PD/WDSF%20Professional%20Division%20Competition%20Rules%20%202012.pdf
- Salsa vs bachata: what's the difference? SalsaVida. Checked 2026-11-04. https://www.salsavida.com/articles/salsa-vs-bachata/
- Tempo and genre. Ableton Learning Music. Checked 2026-11-04. https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/tempo-and-genre.html

# How to keep a dance practice journal: what to track, with prompts

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/
Published: 2026-10-25 · Updated: 2026-10-25 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Corrections fade, small wins get forgotten, and three weeks of classes blur into one. A practice journal keeps them. What to write, a five-minute entry, prompts for when the page stays blank, and how to look back.

Ask a dancer what they worked on three weeks ago and most of us draw a blank. The corrections, the small win in Thursday's class, the section that finally clicked: they all blur together. A practice journal keeps them. It takes five minutes after you dance, and it turns a stack of classes into something you can learn from.

 The short answer

A dance practice journal is a short record you write after every class or practice: the date, what you worked on, one thing that went well, one thing to fix, and a link to the video. Keep each entry to about five minutes, then read back once a week to choose what to focus on next.

- Track: date, class or practice, piece and section, corrections you got, how your body felt, the take you filmed.
- Write: straight after dancing, while the corrections are still in your ears.
- Look back: weekly for patterns, monthly to see how far you've come.

## Why keep a dance diary?

Because memory is a poor record of practice. You remember the class where everything went wrong and forget the five quiet ones where your turns got a little cleaner. A journal evens that out.

There's research behind it, too. A large review of 138 studies found that monitoring your progress towards a goal helps you reach it, and that the effect was larger when the progress was physically recorded rather than just kept in mind.[1] Writing it down is the part that counts.

Practice research points the same way. The work behind the idea of "deliberate practice" describes improvement as effortful practice aimed at specific weaknesses, with feedback.[2] A journal is where those weaknesses get named, and where the feedback from your teacher doesn't evaporate by Saturday.

## What to track in a dance practice journal

Start with the first four rows. Add the rest when writing them feels easy.

| What to note | Example | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Date and kind | Tue, jazz class (75 min) | Shows your real rhythm of practice |
| What you worked on | "Slow Burn", counts 3–4 of the chorus | Lets you find any section's history |
| One win | Double pirouette landed three times in a row | Progress you'd otherwise forget |
| One thing to fix | Arms late on the "and" before 5 | Your focus for next time |
| Corrections you got | "Lift out of the hip in the développé" | Teachers repeat themselves; you'll see which ones |
| The video | Full run, take 2 | The evidence behind the words |
| Body and energy | Tired, left ankle stiff after jumps | Spots overload before it becomes injury |
| Milestones | First clean run of the whole piece | The days you'll want to find again |

Tags help later: the piece, the style, the skill ("turns", "floor work", "musicality"). Keep the list short so you actually use it.

## The five-minute entry, step by step

-

Write it within the hour. On the bus, in the changing room, before you shower. Corrections fade fast.

-

Start with the facts. Date, class or practice, how long, which piece. Thirty seconds.

-

Name one win. Be specific: not "good class" but "kept my heels down in the chassé". Small wins are the point.

-

Name one thing to fix. Only one. A list of ten is a list of none.

-

Copy the correction word for word. Your teacher's exact phrase is often the cue that makes it click later.

-

Attach a take. Even 30 seconds of the section. Words say what you think happened; video shows what did. If you're not filming yet, our guide to [filming yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/) covers the setup.

-

Write tomorrow's first task. "Start with the arm timing in the chorus." Then you walk into the next practice with a plan.

A real entry, start to finish. "Thu 24 Oct, own practice, 40 min, Slow Burn. Win: the turn sequence in the second chorus is finally on the music. Fix: I travel too far on the slide on 6 and arrive late for 7. Teacher's note from Tuesday: 'Smaller, faster, then bigger.' Take: full run, take 3. Body: fine, calves tight. Tomorrow: slide on 6 with a mark on the floor, ten loops."

That's under a hundred words and two minutes of typing. If you practise at home between classes, pair the journal with a simple [weekly practice plan](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-practice-dancing-at-home/), so each entry has something to report back on.

## Journaling prompts for dancers

When the page stays blank, pick one prompt and answer it in two sentences.

- After classWhich correction did I hear twice? What did the teacher demonstrate that I want to steal? What felt different today?
- After your own practiceWhat did the video show that I didn't feel? Which eight-count still needs counting in my head?
- After a performanceWhich moment felt most alive? What did nerves change? What would I keep exactly the same?
- When you feel stuckWhat could I do a month ago that I can do now? (Then go and watch that month-old take.)
- Body checkWhere am I tight, sore or tired? Is it the same place as last week?

## Look back: the weekly and monthly review

A diary nobody reads is just storage. Ten minutes once a week is where the patterns show up.

- Read the weekAll the entries, in order. Which "thing to fix" keeps coming back?
- Watch two takesThe first and last take of the same section this week. Is the fix showing?
- Choose one focusOne skill or section for next week. Write it at the top of the next entry.

Read yesterday's entry before today's practice, too. Sleep seems to help motor skills settle: in a well-known study, people who learned a finger-tapping sequence were about 20% faster after a night's sleep, while the same hours awake brought no significant gain.[3] Dance is far more complex than finger-tapping, but the habit costs nothing: start where yesterday ended, not from scratch.

Once a month, go further back. Put your first take of a piece next to the latest one. That's often the moment you see how much has changed, and it's the raw material for a [dance progress video](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-progress-video/).

## Paper notebook or app?

### A paper notebook

Great forWriting by hand, sketching floor patterns and formations, no screen after class.

Harder atConnecting a note to the video it's about. Searching for "every time I worked on fouettés".

### A dance diary app

Great forKeeping the note, the take and the date together, finding a piece's history in seconds, seeing a month at a glance.

Harder atDrawings and diagrams. Some dancers keep both: the app for takes, a notebook for formations.

A journal, not a scoreboard. Skip streaks and daily quotas; rest days belong in the diary too. If you keep noting the same pain, show your notes to your teacher or a physiotherapist. That's one of the most useful things a journal can do.

## How Dancify keeps the diary for you

Dancify is built around the idea that a dance diary should be made of your own footage. Film a take and a frame from it lands on that day in your calendar; over weeks, the month fills with your own dancing.

-

A calendar of framesEach day shows a frame from what you danced; several takes stack like prints. Free.

-

The day, with notesTakes, notes, tags, favourites and milestones together. Classes can be logged without video.

Pieces keep every take of a choreography in order, the timeline filters by kind of practice, and a month review shows what you danced most. "Log practice" also works from Siri and Shortcuts. The diary is free, there's no account, and it stays on your device or in your own iCloud.

 Start your dance diary

### Five minutes after practice is enough

Film a take or log a class, add one line, and watch the month fill with your own dancing.

- Calendar of frames from your takes
- Notes, tags, favourites, milestones
- Every take of a piece, in order

 [Get Dancify](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6830154598)

## Questions, answered

### What should I write in a dance journal?

The date and kind of practice, what you worked on (piece and section), one thing that went well, one thing to fix, any corrections in your teacher's own words, how your body felt, and a link to the take you filmed. Five minutes is enough.

### How do I track my dance progress?

Combine short notes with video. Film the same section from the same angle regularly, write one line about what changed, and once a month put your first take next to your latest. The notes tell you what to look for; the video shows whether it happened.

### How often should I write in my dance diary?

After every class or practice, ideally within an hour, and keep it short. Then read back once a week for ten minutes and choose one focus for the next week. Rest days can go in too; there's no need for a daily streak.

### Is a paper dance journal or an app better?

Paper is great for handwriting and drawing formations. An app is better at keeping the note, the video and the date together and at finding a piece's history quickly. Many dancers use both.

### Does keeping a practice journal actually help?

Research on goal monitoring says yes: a review of 138 studies found that tracking progress helps people reach their goals, more so when progress is physically recorded. For dancers, the journal also keeps corrections from being forgotten and makes progress visible on slow weeks.

## Sources

- Harkin B, Webb TL, Chang BPI, et al. (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin 142(2), 198–229. Checked 2026-11-04. https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/87431/
- Ericsson KA, Krampe RT, Tesch-Römer C (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review 100(3), 363–406. Checked 2026-11-04. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.100.3.363
- Walker MP, Brakefield T, Morgan A, Hobson JA, Stickgold R (2002). Practice with sleep makes perfect: sleep-dependent motor skill learning. Neuron 35(1), 205–211. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12123620/

# How to practise dance at home: space, warm-up and a weekly plan

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-practice-dancing-at-home/
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-10-23 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> A living room has no teacher, no sprung floor and no plan. Here's how to set up a safe space, warm up, structure a 30-minute session and build a week that improves you without wearing you out.

Class gives you the steps. Home is where they become yours. The trouble is that a living room has no teacher, no sprung floor and no plan, so practice either turns into scrolling for a tutorial or into the same run-through ten times. A little structure fixes most of that.

 The short answer

To practise dance at home, do three to five short sessions a week of 20 to 45 minutes, each with a 10 to 15 minute warm-up, one clear focus, a few targeted drills, a run of your choreography and one recorded take. Clear a safe space, match your footwear to the floor, keep jumps low on hard floors and take at least one or two full rest days a week.

- Floor: wood is kindest; on tile or concrete, cut the jumps. Socks or soft shoes on carpet, bare feet or grippy soles on smooth floors.
- Session: warm up, drill, run, film, cool down.
- Week: mix technique, choreography and conditioning, and leave room to recover.

## Set up a safe space

You need less room than you think: about two by two metres for most technique, more for travelling steps and turns. What matters more is what's around and under you.

Before you start, walk the space. Move anything you could hit or trip on, tape down loose cables, and put fragile things somewhere else. The Imperial Society of Teachers of Dancing (ISTD) recommends exactly this for home dancing, and adds a good habit: walk through your choreography slowly once to find the obstacles before you dance it full out.[1] Check the ceiling too, if your piece has jumps or arm lines overhead.

### Floors, shoes and socks

Studios use sprung floors because they give a little under a landing, which takes some load off ankles, knees and shins. Most home floors don't give at all, so the rule is simple: the harder the floor, the fewer and lower the jumps.

| Floor | What it's like | Wear | Go easy on |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wood or laminate on joists | The best home option: a little give, smooth | Bare feet, dance shoes, socks if you need to turn | Long jump sequences |
| Tile, stone or concrete | Hard, no give, can be slippery | Trainers or dance sneakers with grip | Jumps and kneeling floor work |
| Carpet | Grips the foot, can burn skin | Socks or soft dance shoes | Turns, sliding, knee work without cover |
| Roll-out dance mat or practice board | Studio-like surface on top of your floor | Whatever the style needs (taps on a tap board) | The edges, where you can catch a foot |

The ISTD's footwear advice matches this: grippy soles outdoors and on slippery surfaces, socks or soft dance shoes on carpet, bare feet or grippy dance shoes on smooth indoor floors, and covered skin on carpet or rough surfaces to avoid burns.[1] If a floor is wet or slick, dry it or put down a mat that grips.

## Warm up properly, even for 20 minutes

At home it's tempting to skip the warm-up because there's no teacher starting the barre. Don't. A warm-up should raise your heart rate, mobilise your joints and gently stretch the muscles, gradually, so you don't overdo it before you've started.[1]

-

Raise the heart rate (3–4 minutes). March or jog on the spot, bounce, step-touch to a song you like.

-

Mobilise (3–4 minutes). Circles and rolls through the ankles, knees, hips, spine, shoulders and neck.

-

Move dynamically (4–5 minutes). Leg swings, pliés, lunges with a twist, small grooves in your style.

-

Rehearse the patterns (2 minutes). The movements you're about to drill, small and easy, then bigger.

Keep long held stretches mostly for after practice. In a small study with trained dancers, dynamic stretching or a combination of static and dynamic stretching gave better jump height than static stretching alone, and the combination also gave better balance.[2] Ten dancers is a small study, but it matches what most teachers do: move first, hold later.

## Plan each session

A good home session has one focus. "Clean the turn sequence in the second chorus" is a focus. "Practise" isn't. Here's a 30-minute shape you can stretch to 45:

| Minutes | Block | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 0–10 | Warm-up | Heart rate, joints, dynamic movement |
| 10–18 | Drills | Two or three drills for today's focus, slow then at tempo |
| 18–25 | Choreography | The section you're working on, in small chunks, then joined up |
| 25–27 | One take | Film the section once, full out, from your usual spot |
| 27–30 | Cool-down and note | Easy stretches, then one sentence about what you noticed |

## A weekly plan for beginners and intermediate dancers

These plans assume you also have one or two classes a week. Count a class as a session, and move days around to fit your life. What matters is the mix and the rest.

| Day | Beginner (3 sessions) | Intermediate (4–5 sessions) |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | Technique, 25 min: basics and posture | Technique, 40 min: turns or jumps focus |
| Tue | Class | Class |
| Wed | Rest or a walk | Choreography, 35 min + one take |
| Thu | Choreography, 25 min + one take | Conditioning, 20 min + mobility |
| Fri | Rest | Rest |
| Sat | Class or freestyle, 30 min | Class, or a full run + one take |
| Sun | Rest; watch the week's takes | Freestyle or light technique, 25 min; watch the week's takes |

Add time before you add days. Going from three to five sessions in one week is how overuse injuries start.

## Drills that work in a living room

- Ballet and contemporaryA chair or kitchen counter as a barre: pliés, tendus, relevés and balances. Short, slow and precise beats long and sloppy.
- Hip-hop, heels and commercialGrooves and bounces to a metronome or a single song for three minutes without stopping. Then isolations: head, chest, hips.
- TurnsPrep and spot drills, then quarter and half turns before full ones. Socks on wood if your floor grips too much.
- Choreography and coversLoop one eight-count until it's clean at half speed, then at tempo, then join it to the next one.
- Partner stylesBasics and timing alone: salsa or bachata basic on the beat, frame and arm styling, footwork patterns.
- Tap and IrishRudiments on a practice board at a slow, steady tempo, then faster in small steps.

For choreography, the way you break a piece into chunks matters as much as the time you spend. Our guide to [learning choreography faster](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-learn-choreography-faster/) goes deeper, and [counting music](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-count-music-in-dance/) helps if you lose your place in the song.

## Ten minutes of conditioning

Most dance injuries are in the lower body. In a systematic review of ballet injuries, the lower body (hips, legs, ankles and feet) accounted for 66 to 91 percent of all injuries across the studies.[3] Strong feet, ankles and hips are your best protection, and they need no equipment:

- Calf raises: slow, on both feet then one foot, 2 × 12.
- Single-leg balance: 30 seconds each side, then with eyes closed.
- Glute bridges: 2 × 12, then single-leg.
- Side plank: 20 to 30 seconds each side.
- Foot doming or towel scrunches: one minute each foot.

## Record one take per session

The mirror shows you one angle while you're busy dancing. A recording shows you what actually happened. You don't need to film everything; one take of today's focus, from the same spot every time, is enough. Write one sentence next to it: what improved and what to fix next time.

After a few weeks those takes become something better than motivation: evidence. Keep them in a [practice journal](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/), and when you have a month or two, put the first and the latest side by side as a [progress video](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-progress-video/). If you're unsure about the setup, see [how to film yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/).

## Rest and injury prevention

Home practice comes on top of class, so it's easy to do too much. Most dance injuries come from overuse rather than accidents: in the same review, 75 percent of injuries among amateur ballet dancers were overuse injuries.[3] That's the kind of injury that builds quietly from too many repetitions with too little recovery.

- Take one or two full rest days a week. Light walking and gentle mobility are fine.
- Vary the load. Don't put jumps or deep floor work on consecutive days.
- Sleep counts as practice. In a well-known sleep study, people got about 20 percent faster at a newly learned finger-tapping sequence after a night's sleep, with no such gain after the same time awake. Fingers aren't feet, but the idea that skills settle overnight is a good reason not to cut sleep for extra rehearsal.[4]
- Drink water during practice, not just after.

Stop and get it checked if pain is sharp, if it changes how you move, if there's swelling, or if the same spot still hurts the next morning. A physiotherapist or doctor who works with dancers can tell you what's going on and how to keep dancing safely. This guide is general information, not medical advice.

## Where Dancify fits

 Free in Dancify Loop one section, slowly Set an A–B loop around the eight-count that keeps going wrong, with an optional eight-count pause to get back to your mark. Slow it down to 0.25×, mirror it, and turn on the counts overlay to see 1 to 8 on the music.

-

-

A calendar of framesEach day shows a frame from what you danced, and days without video still get logged.

A musical count-in ("5, 6, 7, 8") gives you time to walk to your mark before the take starts. Recording, the calendar, notes and the editor are free, with no account and no ads; videos stay on your device or in your own iCloud.

## Questions, answered

### How often should I practise dance at home?

Three to five sessions a week of 20 to 45 minutes works for most beginners and intermediate dancers, counting classes as sessions. Beginners can start with three; add time to each session before you add more days, and keep one or two full rest days a week.

### Can I dance on a hard floor at home?

Yes, but adapt. Tile, stone and concrete have no give, so keep jumps few and low, wear trainers or dance sneakers with grip, and avoid kneeling floor work without padding. Wood or laminate is the kindest home floor, and a roll-out dance mat or practice board gives you a studio-like surface on top.

### Should I dance in socks or barefoot at home?

It depends on the floor. The ISTD suggests socks or soft dance shoes on carpet, bare feet or dance shoes with a grippy sole on smooth indoor floors, and shoes with grip on slippery surfaces. On carpet or rough floors, cover your skin to avoid burns.

### How long should a dance warm-up be?

About 10 to 15 minutes. Raise your heart rate, mobilise your joints, move dynamically through your style's patterns and gently stretch, gradually. Keep long held stretches mostly for after practice.

### What should a beginner practise at home?

Basics and posture for your style, short drills at a slow tempo, one small section of choreography until it's clean, and ten minutes of conditioning for feet, ankles and hips. Film one take per session so you can see what's actually changing.

### How do I avoid injury when practising dance at home?

Warm up every time, clear the space, match footwear to the floor, limit jumps on hard floors, increase your practice gradually and take rest days. Most dance injuries are overuse injuries, so recovery matters. See a physiotherapist or doctor if pain is sharp, causes swelling or changes how you move.

## Sources

- Imperial Society of Teachers of Dancing (2021). ISTD Challenge: your health and safety (warm-up, obstructions, floor surfaces, footwear). Checked 2026-11-04. https://www.istd.org/documents/istd-challenge-health-and-safety-guidance/
- Morrin N, Redding E (2013). Acute effects of warm-up stretch protocols on balance, vertical jump height, and range of motion in dancers. Journal of Dance Medicine & Science 17(1), 34–40. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23498355/
- Smith PJ et al. (2015). Incidence and prevalence of musculoskeletal injury in ballet: a systematic review. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 3(7). Checked 2026-11-04. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26673541/
- Walker MP et al. (2002). Practice with sleep makes perfect: sleep-dependent motor skill learning. Neuron 35(1), 205–211. Checked 2026-11-04. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12123620/
