# The best apps for dancers in 2026, by what you need them for

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/best-apps-for-dancers/
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-04 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Classes, filming, slow motion and mirror, counts and tempo, editing and a diary: the apps that do each job well, checked against their own listings, plus the two old favourites that are gone.

There's no single best app for dancers, because dancers need several different things: someone to learn from, a way to see yourself, a way to slow things down, the music under control and somewhere to keep it all. Most of us end up with three or four apps. The trick is choosing ones that each do their job well.

 The short answer

Pick by the job you need done. For most dancers in 2026, a good set is:

- Learning classes: STEEZY, or free YouTube tutorials slowed down and mirrored.
- Recording and reviewing your practice: Dancify (iPhone and iPad), or the built-in Camera and Photos apps for the basics.
- Mirror, slow and loop any video: Dance.io, or the player in Dancify for your own takes.
- Coach-style analysis: OnForm.
- Music and tempo: Anytune to slow a song without changing its pitch, a metronome such as Soundbrenner.
- Editing for social: CapCut, Edits or iMovie.

A note on bias. We make Dancify, so we're not neutral. Every claim about another app here was checked against that company's own website or App Store listing on 4 November 2026, and each one gets credit for what it does better than ours. Sources are at the end. We don't quote prices: they change and differ by country, so check the App Store.

## How we chose

We looked at what dancers actually do in a week: take a class or follow a tutorial, practise a section until it's clean, film it, watch it back, fix the timing, maybe post it. For each job we asked:

- Does it do the job well? Slow motion that's actually slow, a mirror that's one tap away, loops that are easy to set.
- Is it current? Some well-known apps are gone (more on that below), so every app here was available on the App Store when we checked.
- What does it cost you besides money? Accounts, feeds, ads and what happens to your videos.
- Where does it run? Several dancers in a class rarely share one kind of phone.

## Practice apps at a glance

| Feature | We make it Dancify | STEEZY | Dance.io | OnForm | Camera & Photos | CapCut |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Classes or tutorial library | Not available: Bring your own | Paid plan: 1,500+ classes, subscription | Not available: Bring your own | Not available | Not available | Not available |
| Film your practice | Available: Free, with count-in and Follow | Not documented: Webcam mirror in class | Available: Next to the original | Not documented | Available: Free, incl. slo-mo | Not documented |
| Mirror | Available: Free | Available: In classes | Available | Not documented | Available: Flip, as an edit | Not documented |
| Slow motion playback | Available: Down to 0.25×, frame by frame | Available: Tempo control | Available | Available: Fine scrubbing | Available: Speed as an edit | Available: 0.1× to 100×, as an edit |
| Loop a section | Available: A–B loop, free | Available: In classes | Available: A–B loop | Not documented | Not available | Not documented |
| Counts or beat overlay | Available: 1–8 on the music, free | Not documented | Available: Beat overlay | Not documented | Not available | Not documented |
| Two takes side by side | Paid plan only: Premium | Not documented | Available: Compare | Available: Side by side or overlaid | Not available | Not documented |
| Practice diary or calendar | Available: Free | Not documented: Saved classes | Not documented: Notes on moves | Not documented | Not available: Camera roll | Not available |
| Video editor | Available: Free | Not available | Not documented | Not available: Markup and voice-over | Available: Trim, speed, crop | Available: Full editor |
| Runs on (App Store and web) | iPhone, iPad | iPhone, iPad, Android, web | iPhone, iPad, Mac | iPhone, iPad | Built into iPhone and iPad | iPhone, iPad, Mac |

 Available Paid plan Not available or not documented Checked against each provider's website and App Store listing (US), 4 November 2026. STEEZY, Dance.io, OnForm and CapCut are free to download with in-app purchases; which features are paid can change, so check before you subscribe.

## The best app for each job

 Best for learning from classes

### STEEZY

A library of more than 1,500 online classes and programmes from complete beginner up, in styles from hip-hop, heels and K-pop to ballet, contemporary, jazz, salsa and house. Classes can be mirrored, slowed down, looped by section and switched between front and back views, and on a computer a camera mode shows your webcam beside the instructor like a mirror.[1, 2]

Keep in mind: it's a subscription, the app is in English, and it's built for learning their choreography, not for keeping your own practice videos.

 Best free way to learn a routine

### YouTube, plus a mirror extension

Countless free tutorials, and the player can slow any video down to 0.25× in a browser and in the iPhone, iPad and Android apps.[3] On a computer, a browser extension such as Mirror Videos for Chrome adds a mirror button; its listing is written for "lefties and dancers".[4]

Keep in mind: YouTube has no built-in mirror, quality varies hugely, and the recommendations are very good at turning practice into watching.

 Best built-in option

### Apple Camera and Photos

Already on your iPhone. Slo-mo records at up to 240 fps on many models, and in Photos you can trim a clip, change which part plays in slow motion, adjust playback speed and flip a video horizontally.[5, 6, 7]

Keep in mind: no loop, no counts, no live mirror, and practice clips get lost between screenshots and holiday photos.

 Best for mirroring and looping a reference

### Dance.io

A practice player built for copying choreography: A–B loops, speed control, mirror mode, a visual and spoken beat overlay, recording next to the original and a compare view for your own takes against the reference.[8]

Keep in mind: it's a young app from an independent developer, with subscription and lifetime options; it isn't a diary for your practice over time.

 Best for coach-style video analysis

### OnForm

A sports video analysis app with fine scrubbing and slow motion, drawing and voice-over feedback, and two videos side by side or overlaid. Good if a teacher or coach reviews your videos and sends notes back.[9]

Keep in mind: it's built for sport in general, not dance, and the plans for individuals and coaches are subscriptions.

 Best for slowing down the music

### Anytune

Changes a song's tempo without changing its pitch, with loops and marks for the section you're drilling. Its listing names dancers and dance teachers among the people it's made for.[10]

Keep in mind: it works on music files, not video, and it can't play songs protected by streaming services such as Apple Music.

 Best metronome

### The Metronome by Soundbrenner

A clear metronome with time signatures, subdivisions and accents, plus setlists for saved tempos. Useful for drilling grooves, footwork or tap at a steady BPM.[11]

Keep in mind: it's free to download, with extra features in a subscription (Soundbrenner Plus). It's made for musicians, so there are no eight-counts.

 Best for editing short videos

### CapCut

A full editor with speed changes from 0.1× to 100×, speed curves, keyframes, automatic captions and a large library of music and sound effects.[12]

Keep in mind: its App Store privacy label says identifiers may be used to track you across other companies' apps and websites, and user content can be linked to you.

 Best free editor for Reels

### Edits by Instagram

Instagram's editor for iPhone, free to download: single-frame precision, automatic captions, green screen and cutouts, recording up to ten minutes and 4K export without a watermark.[13]

Keep in mind: iPhone only, and it's made with Instagram in mind.

 Best simple editor

### iMovie

Apple's free editor. Trim, split and change clip speed, and put two clips side by side with split screen or in a corner with picture in picture: enough for a simple before and after.[14]

Keep in mind: no counts, loops or practice tools; it's an editor, not a practice app.

 Best for recording, reviewing and remembering your practice

### Dancify

The app we make: a camera, a practice diary and a video editor for dancers, on iPhone and iPad. The camera has a musical count-in, Follow to keep focus on you, a reference video while you film, and slow motion. The player has A–B loops, counts on the music, mirror and 0.25× slow motion. Every take lands on its day in a calendar of frames and on its piece's page. Recording, the diary and the editor are free; Premium adds progress reels, side-by-side compare and a pose guide.

Keep in mind: there are no classes or tutorials, it's iPhone and iPad only, and it's a private tool with no feed or sharing community.

## Apps you'll still see recommended, but can't use

Older lists still recommend two video analysis apps that dancers loved. Neither is available any more:

- Coach's Eye has been retired by TechSmith; its website now says it "is no longer a working service".[15]
- Hudl Technique was sold to the team behind OnForm in May 2021 and discontinued later that year, with a tool to move videos across.[16] If you used it, OnForm is its direct successor.

## Where Dancify fits, honestly

We built Dancify for the part of practice the other apps leave out: what happens after you've learned the steps. You film, you watch, you fix, you film again, and months later you want to see how far you've come. That needs a good camera, a good player and somewhere the takes don't get lost.

 Free in Dancify A practice diary made of your own footage Each day in the calendar shows a frame from what you danced. Log classes without video too, add notes, tags and milestones, and find every take of a piece in order.

- No account, no ads, no tracking
- Videos stay on your device, or in your own iCloud

It pairs well with the others. Learn on STEEZY or YouTube, slow the song in Anytune if you need to, then film your practice in Dancify with the class video playing as a reference. If you want to post a cover, Dancify's editor handles trims, speed, captions and music, or export the take to CapCut or Edits. More on the practice side in our guides to [learning choreography faster](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-learn-choreography-faster/) and [filming yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/).

 For your own practice

### Dancify: a camera, a diary and an editor

If your camera roll is full of practice clips you never watch again, start here. Film with a count-in, review with loops and counts, and see your progress on a calendar.

- Free camera, diary and editor
- Premium for progress reels, compare and the pose guide
- iPhone and iPad, in six languages

## How to choose in two minutes

-

Start with what you lack. No teacher? A class app. A teacher but no feedback between classes? A camera and player for your own takes.

-

Check your phone. On Android, STEEZY and YouTube work; Dancify and the Apple apps don't.

-

Decide where your videos should live. If you'd rather keep practice private, choose an app without a feed or account, and read the privacy label on the App Store.

-

Try the free parts for a real week. Three sessions, not one evening. The right app is the one you open before practice without thinking about it.

## Questions, answered

### What is the best app for dancers in 2026?

It depends on the job. For learning classes, STEEZY. For recording and reviewing your own practice on iPhone or iPad, Dancify. For mirroring, slowing and looping a reference video, Dance.io. For coach-style video analysis, OnForm. For editing short videos, CapCut, Edits or iMovie. Most dancers use two or three of these together.

### What app can mirror and slow down dance videos?

STEEZY can mirror, slow and loop its own classes. Dance.io mirrors, slows and loops any video you bring. YouTube slows videos to 0.25× and a browser extension such as Mirror Videos adds a mirror on a computer. Dancify mirrors, slows to 0.25× and loops your own takes.

### What happened to Coach's Eye?

Coach's Eye has been retired by TechSmith and is no longer a working service. For coach-style analysis with slow motion, drawing and side-by-side comparison, OnForm is a current alternative; for dance practice with a calendar of takes, loops and counts, Dancify is built for that job.

### Is Hudl Technique still available?

No. Hudl sold the Technique app to OnForm in May 2021, and Technique was discontinued later that year. Users were offered a migration tool to move their videos to OnForm.

### What is the best free app to record dance practice?

The built-in Camera and Photos apps on iPhone are free and handle slow motion, trimming and flipping. Dancify's camera, practice diary and editor are free too, and add a musical count-in, Follow, loops and counts; only progress reels, side-by-side compare and the pose guide are Premium.

### Does Dancify have dance classes or tutorials?

No. Dancify is a camera, practice diary and video editor for your own practice, not a class library. Many dancers learn on STEEZY or YouTube and then film and review their practice in Dancify, with the class video playing as a reference while they film. Dancify is available for iPhone and iPad only.

# Why we built a dance practice app with no feed and no scores

URL: https://dancify.studio/blog/why-we-built-dancify/
Published: 2026-10-20 · Updated: 2026-10-20 · By Kasper Koskenvirta

> Dancers film everything and find nothing. Here's why we built Dancify around the camera and a calendar of frames, the decisions behind it, what we left out on purpose and where we're taking it.

Dancers film everything. The warm-up, the combo at the end of class, the third run of the piece, the one where it finally worked. Then the clips sink into the camera roll between screenshots and holiday photos, and when you want to know whether your turns have improved since spring, you scroll for ten minutes and give up. Dancify started with that scroll.

 In short

Dancify is a camera, a practice diary and a video editor for dancers, made by AppRise Ventures, a small team in Espoo, Finland. We built it so that every take has a place, you can practise with it as well as record it, and your progress shows up in your own footage.

- The camera, calendar, notes and editor are free. Premium is only for progress tools.
- No account, no feed, no followers, no ads. Your videos stay yours.
- No streaks, no likes and no scores. Practice and memory, not points.

## Filmed everything, found nothing

Watching yourself is one of the most useful things a dancer can do. Teachers have known it for as long as there have been cameras in studios, and research on video self-evaluation backs it up.[1] Phones made filming free. They didn't make it useful.

A camera roll is built for photos of moments, not for a practice that runs over months. It doesn't know which clip belongs to which piece, which take was the good one, or what you were working on that day. So the most honest record of your dancing ends up as clutter, and the question "am I getting better?" gets answered by feel.

We wanted the opposite: a place where filming practice and remembering it are the same action.

## Six decisions that shaped Dancify

- Camera first Record is one tap away from the calendar, or one sentence to Siri, because a practice diary that needs typing gets skipped. The camera is made for dancing: a musical count-in so you can walk to your mark, Follow to keep focus and exposure on you as you move, slow motion, mirror, and recording from the volume buttons.
- A calendar of frames Each day in the calendar shows a frame from what you danced. A month of practice looks like a contact sheet, and an empty week looks quiet, never red. Classes and rehearsals without video get logged too.
- Tools for practising, not just recording A reference video while you film, starting on the count-in's downbeat. An A–B loop with an optional eight-count pause. Counts from 1 to 8 laid over the music. These are the things a dancer reaches for in the middle of a session, not afterwards.
- Private by design No account to create and nothing to post. Videos and the diary stay on your device, or in your own private iCloud if you switch sync on, where we can't see them. The App Store privacy label reads Data Not Collected.[2]
- A free editor Frame-accurate trims, speed changes and ramps, freeze frames, crop and colour, titles, captions, a date stamp and music. Exports become a new take; the original is never changed. Editing your own practice shouldn't cost extra.
- Premium only for progress Dancify Premium adds progress reels (first try to latest, with dates), side-by-side compare and a pose guide. Everything you need to film, practise and keep a diary stays free.

 Free in Dancify Why the calendar shows frames, not dots Dots and heatmaps tell you how often you practised. Frames remind you what you practised: the costume from the showcase, the barre in the old studio, the evening the turn finally landed. Strips of coloured tape, like spike tape on a stage floor, mark classes, rehearsals and practice.

## What we left out on purpose

Some features would probably make an app grow faster. We think they would make Dancify worse at its job.

### Not in Dancify

A social feedPractice footage is unfinished on purpose. It shouldn't have to be good enough for an audience.

Likes and followersYou'd start filming for them instead of for yourself.

StreaksRest days are part of training. A broken chain shouldn't make you feel you've failed.

AI scoresA number can't tell you whether you meant the music. The pose guide draws lines over your body to help you see; it doesn't grade you.

### What we built instead

Your own archiveEvery take on its day and in its piece, and on a timeline you can filter.

Notes and milestonesOne sentence after a session, a star on the day it clicked.

Then and nowYour first try next to your latest, with the dates.

Sharing when you chooseExport a take or a reel, save it to Photos and send it where you like.

Progress in dance is quiet. We wanted an app that's quiet too, and then shows you, in your own footage, how far you've come.

## Made for every style

A ballet or contemporary dancer can check lines at the barre. A hip-hop, heels or K-pop dancer can loop the eight-count that won't stick. Salsa and ballroom couples can film their basics, and tap and Irish dancers can slow their footwork to a quarter of the speed. The tools are the same; the camera height changes. Our guide to [filming yourself dancing](https://dancify.studio/blog/how-to-film-yourself-dancing/) covers that part.

It runs on iPhone and iPad (iOS and iPadOS 26 or later), including the iPhone Duo, where the panes sit on either side of the fold. The app speaks English, German, Finnish, Spanish, French and Japanese. Siri and Shortcuts can start a recording, log a practice, open today or show progress for a piece. With an external display or AirPlay, the open take plays full screen on the big screen, which is handy in a studio.

-

A camera that waits for the countCount-in, Follow, slow motion, mirror, grid and level.

-

An editor that's freeTrim, speed, freeze, crop, colour, captions and music. The original stays untouched.

## How Dancify pays for itself

We're a small company, so we'd rather be clear about this. Dancify is free to download, with no ads and no data to sell. Dancify Premium, yearly with a one-week free trial or monthly, unlocks progress reel export, side-by-side compare and the pose guide. That's the whole business model. If Premium isn't for you, the free app is still a complete camera, practice diary and editor.

## What's next

We'll keep refining the core before we add more: the camera, the calendar and the practice tools, shaped by what dancers tell us they need in the middle of a session. The principles won't change: your videos stay yours, practice is never turned into a score, and the free app stays complete.

We won't promise dates we can't keep. We'll write about what we build here on the blog, alongside guides like [keeping a dance practice journal](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-practice-journal/) and [making a progress video](https://dancify.studio/blog/dance-progress-video/). And if something in Dancify feels wrong, or you're missing something, [write to us](mailto:appriseven@gmail.com). We read every message.

## Questions, answered

### Who makes Dancify?

Dancify is designed and built by AppRise Ventures Oy, a small company in Espoo, Finland. The app is available for iPhone and iPad, in English, German, Finnish, Spanish, French and Japanese.

### What's free in Dancify, and what's Premium?

Recording, the calendar and timeline, notes, tags, milestones, the practice tools (count-in, reference video, A–B loop, counts), the video editor and iCloud sync are free. Dancify Premium, yearly with a one-week free trial or monthly, adds progress reel export, side-by-side compare and the pose guide.

### Do I need an account to use Dancify?

No. There's no account, no sign-in and no profile. Your videos and diary stay on your device, or in your own private iCloud if you turn sync on. The App Store privacy label is Data Not Collected.

### Does Dancify use AI to score my dancing?

No. Dancify doesn't score or rank dancing. The optional pose guide (Premium) uses Apple's Vision framework on your device to draw lines over shoulders, hips and balance so you can see your alignment; nothing is uploaded and nothing is graded.

### Why doesn't Dancify have a social feed or streaks?

Practice footage is meant to be unfinished, and rest days are part of training. A feed would make you film for an audience, and streaks would make a rest day feel like failure. You can still export and share any take or reel when you choose.

### Is Dancify available on Android?

No. Dancify is built natively for iPhone and iPad running iOS or iPadOS 26 or later, including the iPhone Duo. There's no Android or web version.
